It is evident from what has now appeared, that in

It is fuppofed above, that two of the conditions of a

Principle, in fcience, is a truth, admitted without Principle,
proof, from which other truths are inferred by a chain of , ringle-j
reafoning. Principles are of two Winte, primary ^ge¬
neral; and to the laft the name of axioms is ufually given
on account of their importance and dignity.. An axiom
or general principle, when the terms in which it is ex-
preffed are underftood, muft be a felf-evident truth ; but
from its very nature it cannot be 's.firjl truth. Our fiift
truths are all particular. A child knows tnat two par¬
ticular lines, each an inch long, are equal to one an¬
other, before he has formed any general notions of
length and equality. “ Things equal to. one and the
fame thing are equal to one another,” is the firft of
Euclid’s axioms ; and an axiom it undoubtedly is, but
to no man has it been zfrfl truth. It is, if we may u e
the expreflion, a genus or clafs of truths, comprehending
under it numberlefs individuals. Were a full-grown
man introduced into the world, without a fingle idea in
his mind, as we may fuppofe Adam to have been, he
would inftantly perceive, upon laying together three
pieces of wood each a foot long, that they were all equal
in length ; and if he were to cut another to the fame
length with any one of them, he would find upon trial
that it was of the fame length with them all. After a
few fimple experiments of this kind,.he would, by a law
of human thought, infer, that all things equal in .length
or in any other dimenfion, to any one thing, are in that
dimenfion equal to one another.
It was not therefore with fuch weaknefs as lome
have imagined, that Hobbes affirmed thofe propofitions
commonly called axioms, not to be primary but iecon-
dary principles. A primary principle deferves not the
name of an axiom, as it is only a particular truth in¬
cluding in it no other truth. There is not one ot Eu¬
clid’s axioms which has not been the refultof indudhon,
though we remember not the time at which the induc¬
tion was made. That the whole is greater than any
of its parts is a general truth which no man of com¬
mon fenfe can controvert ; but every one difcovered
that truth by obferving that his body was larger th«m
his head, his foot, or his hand.; that a mountain is
larger than a mole-hill in the middle of it; and that a
piece of timber meafuring Avhat is called a yard is. longer
than any one of the divifions marked upon it, and
termed inches. The particular obfervations are made

vides them into demonjlrations, proofs, and probabilities.

Hardly any thing is fufceptible of ftrift demonftration
befides the mathematical fciences, and a few propofitiens
in metaphyfical'theology. Phyfics reft upon principles,

wife expeft to happen again j but our expectation is not
confident. Uniform exjierience is proof j frequent expe¬
rience is probability. The ftrongeft man has always been
able to lift the greateft weight j and, therefore, knowing
that one man is ftronger than another, we expedt, with
confidence, that the former will lift more than the lat¬
ter. The belt difciplined army has generally proved

therefore expedt that an army of veterans will, upon fair
ground, defeat an equal number of new levied troops:

foldiers, this expectation is accompanied with doubt,
and the utmoft that we can fay of the expedted event is,
that it is probable ; whereas in the competition between

as confiftent with their knowledge,’ their teftirpony

SECTION IL
Of the Orthographic ProjeElion of the Sphere.
The orthographic projedtion of the fphere, is that in
which the eye is placed in the axis of the plane of pro-
jedtion, at an infinite diftance with refpedl to the dia¬
meter of the fphere j fo that at the fphere all the vifual
rays are aflumed parallel, and therefore perpendicular to
the plane of projedtion.
Hence the orthographic projedtion of any point is
where a perpendicular from that point meets the plane
of projedlion ; and the orthographic reprefentation of
any objedt is the figurd formed by perpendiculars draw n
from every point of the objedt to the plane of pro-
jedlion.
This method of projection is ufed in the geometrical
delineation of eclipfes, occultations, and tranlits. It is
alfo particularly ufeful in various other projections, fuch
as the analemma. See Geography, &c.
Proposition I. Theorem I.
Every ftraight line is projected into a ftraight line. If
the given line be parallel to the plane of projection,
it is projected into an equal ftraight line j but if it is
inclined to the primitive, then the given ftraight line
will be to its projection in the ratio of the radius to
the cofine of inclination.
Let AB (fig. 27.) be the plane of projection, andp^
let CD be a ftraight line parallel thereto: from the ex- b '
tremities C, D of the ftraight line CD, draw' the lines
CE, DF perpendicular to AB 5 then by 3. of xi. of
Eucl. the interfedlion EF, of the plane CEFD, with
the plane of projection, is a ftraight line : and becaufe
the ftraight lines CD, EF are parallel, and alfo CE,
DF j therefore by 34. of i. of Eucl. the oppofite fides
are equal 3 hence the ftraight line CD, and its projec¬
tion EF, are equal. Again, let GH be the propofed
ftraight line, inclined to the primitive j then the lines
GE, HF being drawn perpendicular to AB, the inter¬
cepted portion EF will be the projection of GH.
Through G draw GI parallel to AB, and the angle
IGH will be equal to the inclination of the given line
to the plane of projection. Now GH being the radius,
GI, or its equal EF, will be the cofine of IGH ; hence
the given line GH is to its projection EF as radius to
the cofine or inclination.

Of the Gnomonic Projection of the Sphere.
In this projection the eye is in the centre of the
fphere, and the plane of projeCHon touches the fphere
in a given point parallel to a given circle. It is named
gnomonic, on account of its being the foundation of di¬
alling : the plane of projection may alfo reprefent the
plane of a dial, whofe centre being the projected pole,
the femiaxis of the fphere will be the ftile or gnomon
of the dial.
As the projection of great circles is reprefented by
ftraight lines, and lefs circles parallel to the plane of
projection are projected into concentric circles : there-
fere many problems of the fpbere are very eafily refol-
ved. Other problems, however, become more intricate
on account of feme of the circles being projected into
ellipfes, parabolas, and hyperbolas.

RATIO, in Arithmetic and Geometry, is that rela¬
tion of homogeneous things which determines the quan¬
tity of one from the quantity of another, without the in¬
tervention of a third.
The numbers, lines, or quantities, A and B, being
propofed, their relation one to another may be confider-
ed under one of thefe two heads : 1. Flow much A ex¬
ceeds B, or B exceeds A ? And this is found by taking
A from B, or B from A, and is called arithmetic rca-
fon or ratio. 2. Or how many times, or parts of a
time, A contains B, or B contains A ? and this is cal¬
led geometric reafon or ratio ; (or, as Euclid defines it,
it is the mutual habitude, or refpett, of two magnitudes
of the fame kind, according to quantity 5 that is, as to
how often the one contains, or is contained in, the
other) ; and is found by dividing A by B, or B by
A. And here note, that that quantity which is referred
to another quantity is called the antecedent of tha ratio:
and that to which the other is referred is called thec'ys-
feejuent of the ratio ; as in the ratio of A to B, A is
the antecedent, and B the confequent. Therefore any
quantity, as antecedent, divided by any quantity as a
confe.quent, gives the ratio of that antecedent to the
eonfequent.
Thus the ratio of A to B is —, but the ratio of B

Thus aline, how {hurt foevcr, may be multiplied, that is,

The manner in which the comparifon is made, is this.
When a body advances in a fluid with a known velocity,
it puts a known quantity of the fluid into motion (as is
fuppofed) with this velocity; and this is done in a known
time. We have only to examine what weight will put
this quantity of fluid into the fame motion, by adting on
it during the fame time. This weight is conceived as
equal to the refiftance. Thus, let us fuppofe that a

putting eight cubic feet ,of water into motion with this
velocity ; and doing this by adting uniformly during a
fecond. What weight is able to produce this effedt ?
The weight of eight feet of water, adting during a fe¬
cond on it, will, as is well known, give it the velocity
of thirty-two feet per fecond ; that is, four times greater.
Therefore, the weight of the fourth part of eight cubic
feet, that is, the weight of two cubic feet, adling dur¬
ing a fecond, w’ill do the fame thing, or the weight of
a column of water whofe bafe is a fquare foot, and
whofe height is two feet. This will not only produce

folid body, but it will alfo do it by the fame degrees, as

fourth of its weight, and comparing this with the gra¬

the progrefs of the refitted furface.
Now it is well known that eight cubic feet of water,
